narrativeStructure: A world forms; much later, people ask what lies beyond its sky.
V1 and V2 wartime weapons lead to postwar rocketry, the Space Race, orbital flight and a dated lunar goal.
Apollo sends the Eagle lunar lander toward the surface while Columbia remains in orbit; Armstrong’s first step follows.
Enterprise’s atmospheric tests introduce the Shuttle, its scientific work, losses and retirement after ISS assembly.
International cooperation builds the International Space Station, and Soyuz keeps its crews arriving after Shuttle retirement.
Voyager, Philae and Rosetta carry instruments to distant destinations; both Rosetta and Philae remain on comet 67P.
Returning launchers in 2019/2020 precede Perseverance and Webb in 2021. An explicitly identified present-tense epilogue then reflects on the traces left on the Moon and Mars.
editorialChanges: The war narration names V1 then V2 and transitions to the postwar space programmes; the displayed footage is dated separately.
The Space Race / La course à l’espace replaces the earlier chapter wording.
An additional eight seconds of moving Yuri Gagarin imagery carries music without extra dialogue or labels.
Historical event dates are displayed with source-specific context recorded below.
The Moon objective is dated 25 May 1961; Apollo is explicitly called a programme.
Eagle is identified as the lunar lander and Columbia as the command module before descent and the first step.
Enterprise aboard the Boeing 747 appears in 1977 before the first orbital Shuttle launch in 1981.
The final Shuttle landing accompanies the 2004 retirement decision, completed ISS assembly, cost and safety context, and the last flight in 2011.
Soyuz transport is connected to the end of Shuttle flights; the film does not claim Soyuz stopped flying in 2020.
ESA’s existing animation illustrates Rosetta’s controlled descent in 2016. No fictional takeoff is shown.
The ending dissolves the Solar System picture to black, then introduces the centered RELIC symbol, wordmark and a thin rule.
The player switches English/French at the current playhead and preserves volume, captions, speed and play/pause state. The H control and shortcut are removed.
Enterprise precedes the Voyager launches; Falcon 2019/2020 precedes Perseverance and Webb 2021. The legacy montage is explicitly identified as an epilogue.
endingTreatment: The final held Solar System picture fades to black over 1.4 seconds. The centered symbol and RELIC wordmark enter in sequence, followed by a short thin rule. Timing follows the media clock and remains correct after seeking. Reduced-motion preferences use a static black brand card. No new dialogue is added.

catalogContext: The inherited catalogue documents licensed source research, including material used in previous edits. Only editTimeline and its file references identify pictures delivered in this V9 edition. currentAdditionalSources includes new footage and primary date references; an event reference is not itself a claim that its page supplied the displayed footage.
spaceXContext: The 2019 STP-2 Falcon Heavy and 2020 Sentinel-6 Falcon 9 archive shots precede Perseverance and Webb in 2021. SpaceX’s founding in 2002 is biographical context; these shots do not claim to show the first booster recoveries.
historicalContext: Civilian rocketry predates the Second World War. V1 was a cruise missile; V2 was a ballistic rocket. The selected V2 archive shows captured hardware tested at White Sands in 1946, while narration dates wartime deployment to 1944.
The moving von Braun archive was filmed in 1962 and illustrates a postwar career described by the narration.
Sputnik was the first artificial satellite, launched 4 October 1957. The selected preserved flight spare was filmed later. The archived radio signal is genuine.
Laika was the first dog in orbit, not the first dog sent above the atmosphere. She did not survive. The source illustrates her with a historical portrait.
Gagarin became the first human in space on 12 April 1961. The added eight seconds contain images and music only.
Kennedy proposed the lunar goal on 25 May 1961. The retained Rice University speech was delivered on 12 September 1962.
Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969. Eagle landed on 20 July. Armstrong’s first step occurred on 21 July UTC, still 20 July in the United States.
Enterprise was an atmospheric test orbiter. Its 1977 Boeing 747 carrier footage predates Columbia’s first orbital Shuttle flight on 12 April 1981.

The Shuttle retirement decision was announced in 2004. Completion of ISS assembly, programme cost and safety influenced the transition. Atlantis landed on the final Shuttle mission on 21 July 2011. Challenger in 1986 was not the final Shuttle flight; Columbia was also lost in 2003.
Crewed stations existed before the ISS. The 1998 passage introduces assembly of the International Space Station, followed by Europe’s Columbus module in 2008 and a 2009 full-station flyaround.
Soyuz carried every arriving ISS crew between the final Shuttle flight and Crew Dragon’s first crewed launch in 2020. Soyuz continued to fly after 2020.
Voyager probes launched in 1977. Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause on 25 August 2012; it has not left the Oort cloud or all solar gravitational influence.

Philae first touched comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko on 12 November 2014 as part of ESA’s Rosetta mission. Rosetta ended its mission in a controlled descent on 30 September 2016. Both remain on the comet. This was an ESA-led mission, not a NASA landing, and Rosetta is not the comet’s name.
Falcon Heavy STP-2 on 25 June 2019 and Falcon 9 / Sentinel-6 on 21 November 2020 precede Perseverance on 18 February 2021 and Webb on 25 December 2021.
The ending joins existing mission and visualization videos; it is not a physically continuous camera recording from a rover to the entire Solar System.
